bib.title: Clean Code, Chapter 12: Emergence
bib.venue: Clean Code: A Handbook of Agile Software Craftsmanship, Prentice Hall (guest chapter, pp. 171-176)

question: Can Kent Beck's four rules of Simple Design guide a developer to good designs as the code is written?
hypothesis: Following the four rules makes good design emerge and makes principles such as SRP and DIP easier to apply.
contributions: Presents Beck's four rules of Simple Design in priority order and explains how each pushes design quality
Worked refactorings for duplication: replaceImage extraction and Template Method

results.claim: Beck's four rules of Simple Design, in order of importance: runs all the tests, no duplication, expresses intent, minimizes classes and methods.
results.setup: Rules applied during incremental refactoring of code that has tests
results.quote: The rules are given in order of importance.
results.note: Order differs from Fowler's wording (tests, intention, duplication, fewest elements).

results.claim: Making a system testable pushes design toward small, single-purpose classes and lower coupling (DIP, dependency injection).
results.quote: Writing tests leads to better designs.

results.claim: Duplication is called the primary enemy of a well-designed system; it includes duplicated implementation, not just identical lines.
results.setup: Examples: isEmpty() defined as 0 == size(); replaceImage extracted from scaleToOneDimension and rotate
results.quote: Duplication is the primary enemy of a well-designed system.

results.claim: Extracting commonality in tiny pieces exposes SRP violations and enables reuse in the small, which can shrink complexity.
results.quote: This “reuse in the small” can cause system com-
results.note: Quote ends at a line break (text continues 'plexity to shrink dramatically').

results.claim: Template Method removes higher-level duplication: subclasses fill the only non-duplicated step (alterForLegalMinimums).
results.setup: VacationPolicy with US and EU subclasses
results.quote: We can eliminate the obvious duplication by applying the TEMPLATE METHOD pattern.

results.claim: Code should express intent, because most project cost is long-term maintenance; means: good names, small functions and classes, standard pattern names, expressive tests, and effort.
results.quote: The majority of the cost of a software project is in long-term maintenance.

results.claim: The most important way to be expressive is to try; the likely next reader is you.
results.quote: But the most important way to be expressive is to try.

results.claim: The fourth rule guards against over-decomposition and dogma (an interface per class, data/behavior class split) but is lowest priority.
results.quote: High class and method counts are sometimes the result of pointless dogmatism.

results.claim: Simple-design practices cannot replace experience but compress it.
results.quote: Is there a set of simple practices that can replace experience? Clearly not.

limits: No data or evidence: all claims are assertion and worked examples
Never mentions YAGNI, the wrong abstraction, or when duplication is acceptable; treats duplication as always to be removed
Duplication examples are Java; Template Method uses inheritance
Rule 4 is only briefly argued; no measure of 'too many' classes
practices: Write tests and run them continuously; testability pushes toward small classes and low coupling (p. 172).
After each few lines added, pause, refactor and rerun tests (p. 172).
Eliminate duplication even in a few lines, including duplicated implementation (pp. 173-174).
Use Template Method for higher-level duplication (p. 174).
Choose good names, keep functions and classes small, use standard pattern names, write expressive tests (p. 175).
Resist dogmas that inflate class counts, such as an interface for every class (p. 176).

terms.definition: A design is simple if it runs all the tests, contains no duplication, expresses the intent of the programmer, and minimizes the number of classes and methods.
Extracting tiny shared methods, possibly into other classes, so others can reuse them; essential to reuse in the large.
